Text: Chromosomes are composed of two types of macromolecules: {{c1::nucleic acids}} and {{c1::proteins}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the classic 1940s–50s experiments (Avery's transformation work, Hershey–Chase) established that the genetic information lives in the nucleic acids, not the proteins.

Cue: the two kinds of nucleic acid are DNA and RNA.

Text: In Griffith's experiment, mice injected with a mix of heat-killed virulent Type IIIS and living avirulent Type IIR pneumococci {{c1::died of pneumonia}}, and {{c1::living Type IIIS}} cells were recovered from their carcasses.
Back Extra:
Cue: neither part alone kills — the IIIS cells are dead and the living IIR strain is avirulent.

Why: something heritable must have passed from the dead IIIS cells into the living IIR cells.

Text: The unknown agent from heat-killed Type IIIS cells that converted living Type IIR cells into Type IIIS was named the {{c1::“transforming principle”::historic term}} — the conversion changed the cells' {{c2::hereditary material::what kind of material}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the conversion is genetic, not a temporary change in appearance — the transformed cells breed true as Type IIIS.

Text: In {{c1::1931::year}}, {{c1::Richard Sia and Martin Dawson::two researchers}} showed that pneumococcal transformation happens {{c2::in vitro — the mice played no role::where}}.
Back Extra:
Why: Griffith's original experiment ran inside mice; showing the same conversion in a culture dish proved the animal contributed nothing.

Cue: their in vitro system set the stage for Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: {{c1::Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty::three researchers}} showed that {{c2::DNA::molecule}} is the only component of Type IIIS cells able to transform Type IIR cells into Type IIIS.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Griffith discovered THAT transformation happens; Avery's team identified WHAT does the transforming.

Cue: the purified transforming extract kept working after protein and RNA were destroyed — only destroying DNA stopped it.

Text: To rule out protein contamination of their DNA extract, Avery's team used specific enzymes to destroy one candidate molecule at a time: transforming activity survived {{c1::protease}} and {{c1::RNase}} treatment but was eliminated entirely by {{c1::DNase}}.
Back Extra: Why: each enzyme degrades exactly one macromolecule, so the treatment that kills the activity names the molecule carrying it.

Text: A cell-free bacterial extract carries genetic information of unknown molecular identity. Treating it with DNase destroys the activity, while protease and RNase leave it intact. The information is stored in {{c1::DNA::molecule}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the logic runs backward from destruction — whichever single enzyme abolishes the activity, its substrate is the carrier.

Text: Proof that DNA is the genetic material of bacteriophage T2 was published in {{c1::1952::year}} by {{c1::Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase::two researchers}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: Hershey went on to win the 1969 Nobel Prize.

Distinguish: Avery's team proved it by transformation in pneumococcus; Hershey and Chase proved it by radioactive labeling of a phage.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The Hershey–Chase labeling strategy exploits one chemical difference: {{c1::phosphorus::element}} is found in DNA but virtually absent from protein, while {{c1::sulfur::element}} is found in protein but absent from DNA.
Back Extra: Why: with an element unique to each macromolecule, a radioactive isotope of that element tags one molecule cleanly.

Text: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, growing phage in medium with radioactive {{c1::³²P::isotope}} labeled the phage {{c2::DNA}}, and growing them with radioactive {{c1::³⁵S::isotope}} labeled the phage {{c2::protein coats}}.
Back Extra: Why: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur; protein contains sulfur but virtually no phosphorus.

Text: Hershey and Chase found that the phage's {{c1::DNA}} entered the E. coli cell, while most of the phage's {{c1::protein}} remained adsorbed to the outside of the cell.
Back Extra:
Why: progeny viruses are assembled inside the cell, so whatever entered must carry the instructions for building them — the genetic material is the DNA.

Ex: progeny particles carried some of the parental ³²P but none of the ³⁵S.

Text: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, shearing ³⁵S-labeled infected cells in a blender removed most of the radioactivity {{c1::without affecting::with or without affecting}} progeny phage production.
Back Extra:
Why: the sheared-off material was empty protein coats — reproduction runs entirely on the DNA already inside the cell.

Distinguish: with ³²P-labeled phage, essentially all the radioactivity stayed inside the cells and could not be sheared away.

Text: The loose end in Hershey and Chase's proof — a significant amount of {{c1::³⁵S (protein)::isotope}} entered the cells with the DNA — was closed by {{c2::transfection}} experiments, in which E. coli {{c2::protoplasts::cell preparation}} infected with pure phage DNA yield normal progeny phage.
Back Extra:
Why: if naked DNA alone produces complete infective progeny, no protein contaminant can be the genetic material.

Cue: a protoplast is a cell with its wall removed.

Text: Most living organisms store their genetic information in {{c1::DNA}}; some viruses instead store it in {{c2::RNA}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: those viruses contain RNA and proteins but no DNA at all.

Why: every organism studied stores its genetic information in a nucleic acid — never in protein.

Text: RNA was established as the genetic material of RNA viruses by the {{c1::reconstitution}} experiment of {{c1::Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat::researcher}} and coworkers, published in {{c1::1957::year}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the experiment mixed and matched the two components of tobacco mosaic virus — protein coat from one strain, RNA from another.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Fraenkel-Conrat reconstituted hybrid TMV particles from the {{c1::protein coat}} of one strain and the {{c1::RNA}} of a different strain; the progeny viruses were always identical to the strain that donated the {{c2::RNA::protein coat or RNA}}.
Back Extra:
Why: offspring follow the nucleic acid, not the coat — so TMV's genes are its RNA.

Cue: TMV contains no DNA at all, just one RNA molecule in a protein coat.
verified_by: answer_in_stem cleared: c2 is a forced choice between the two components the stem must name; recall is which one, not the word

Text: In {{c1::1868::year}}, {{c1::Johann Friedrich Miescher::person}} isolated an acidic, phosphorus-rich substance from pus cells and named it {{c2::“nuclein”}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: Miescher’s “nuclein” is what we now call nucleic acid — 1868 marks its first isolation.

Cue: a skeptical journal editor repeated the experiments himself, delaying publication until 1871.

Why: nitrogen and phosphorus together was an oddity — at the time the pair was known to coexist only in certain fats.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The role of nucleic acids in storing and transmitting genetic information was not established until {{c1::1944::year}}; the double-helix structure itself followed in 1953.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Miescher had isolated nuclein back in 1868 — it took ~75 years to prove what it was for.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The repeating subunit of a nucleic acid is the {{c1::nucleotide}}.
Back Extra: Cue: a poly-nucleotide chain is just many of these joined in a row.

Text:
Each nucleotide is composed of three parts:

{{c1::a phosphate group}}

{{c1::a five-carbon sugar (pentose)}}

{{c1::a cyclic, nitrogen-containing base}}
Back Extra: Cue: sugar + base + phosphate — the sugar sits in the middle, bridging the other two.

Text: The pentose sugar in DNA is {{c1::2-deoxyribose}}; in RNA it is {{c1::ribose}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the names carry the answer — DEOXYribonucleic acid vs RIBOnucleic acid.

Distinguish: deoxyribose lacks the hydroxyl (OH) group at the 2′ carbon that ribose carries.
verified_by: husk_groups cleared: each blank is cued by its own key (DNA vs RNA), answerable with the other hidden

Text:
The four bases commonly found in DNA are:

{{c1::adenine (A)}}

{{c1::guanine (G)}}

{{c1::thymine (T)}}

{{c1::cytosine (C)}}
Back Extra: Distinguish: RNA keeps A, G, and C but swaps thymine for uracil.

Text: RNA contains the base {{c1::uracil (U)}} in place of DNA's {{c1::thymine (T)}}.
Back Extra: Cue: U replaces T — the other three bases (A, G, C) are shared by both nucleic acids.

Text: The double-ring bases, called {{c2::purines}}, are {{c1::adenine and guanine::2 bases}}.
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: PURe As Gold — the two purines are A and G.

Distinguish: purines have two rings but only two members; pyrimidines have one ring and three members.

Text: The single-ring bases, called {{c2::pyrimidines}}, are {{c1::cytosine, thymine, and uracil::3 bases}}.
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: CUT the PY — the pyrimidines are C, U, and T.

Cue: DNA uses C and T; RNA uses C and U.

Text: RNA usually exists as a {{c1::single::single or double}}-stranded polymer, whereas DNA is usually {{c1::double::single or double}}-stranded.
Back Extra: Pitfall: “usually” matters — some viral genomes break the pattern (ΦX174 packages single-stranded DNA).
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: In {{c1::1953::year}}, {{c1::James Watson and Francis Crick::two researchers}} deduced that DNA is a right-handed double helix — two polynucleotide chains coiled about one another in a spiral.
Back Extra: Cue: the model rested on two kinds of evidence — Chargaff's base chemistry and Wilkins & Franklin's X-ray diffraction data.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The 1962 Nobel Prize for the double helix went to Watson, Crick, and {{c1::Maurice Wilkins::third laureate}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray data were central, died in 1958 at age 37 — and Nobel Prizes are never awarded posthumously.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: When Erwin Chargaff analyzed DNA from many different organisms, the concentration of thymine always equaled that of {{c1::adenine}}, the concentration of cytosine always equaled that of {{c1::guanine}}, and total purines always equaled total {{c2::pyrimidines}}.
Back Extra: Why: fixed pairwise ratios hinted that T sits with A and C sits with G in some fixed physical relationship — the base pairs Watson and Crick then modeled.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: Double-stranded DNA that is 33% guanine has an adenine content of {{c1::17%::percent}}.
Back Extra:
Pathway: %G = %C → G+C = 66% → A+T = 100−66 = 34% → A = 17%.

Pitfall: this arithmetic is only legal for DOUBLE-stranded nucleic acid — single strands have no strict pairing.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Chargaff-style base arithmetic (%A from %G) fails for the DNA packaged in phage ΦX174, because that DNA is {{c1::single::single or double}}-stranded.
Back Extra:
Why: with only one strand there is no strict A=T / G=C base pairing to compute from.

Pitfall: exam stems love this trap — check WHETHER the nucleic acid is double-stranded before using A=T and G=C.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: The X-ray diffraction data behind the double-helix model came from {{c1::Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin::two researchers}}, and showed a highly ordered, two-stranded structure with repeats every 0.34 nm along the axis.
Back Extra: Cue: the cross-shaped diffraction pattern says “helix”; the strong top/bottom bands say “stacked bases, 0.34 nm apart.”
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Within one DNA strand, adjacent nucleotides are joined by covalent {{c1::phosphodiester}} bonds; the two strands of the helix are held together by {{c2::hydrogen}} bonds between opposing bases.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: strong covalent bonds build the backbone; individually weak (but numerous) hydrogen bonds zip the strands together.

Cue: a phosphodiester linkage runs C—O—P—O—C, joining the 5′ carbon of one sugar to the 3′ carbon of the next.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: Watson–Crick base pairing is specific: adenine always pairs with {{c1::thymine}}, and guanine always pairs with {{c1::cytosine}} — so every base pair consists of one {{c2::purine}} and one {{c2::pyrimidine}}.
Back Extra: Why: the pairing is set by the bases' hydrogen-bonding capacities in their normal configurations — A cannot hydrogen-bond with C, nor T with G.

Text: A–T base pairs form {{c1::two::number of}} hydrogen bonds; G–C pairs form {{c1::three::number of}}.
Back Extra: Why: the third bond makes G:C-rich DNA denser and harder to pull apart.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Because base pairing is strict, the sequence of one DNA strand fixes the sequence of the other — the two strands are said to be {{c1::complementary}}.
Back Extra: Why: complementarity is what makes DNA uniquely suited to store and transmit genetic information — each strand can serve as the template for rebuilding the other during replication.

Text: One DNA strand reads 5′-ATCG-3′. Written in the conventional 5′→3′ direction, its complementary strand is {{c1::5′-CGAT-3′}}.
Back Extra:
Pathway: pair each base (TAGC), then read the new strand from ITS OWN 5′ end — i.e., reverse it.

Pitfall: writing TAGC forgets the reversal; the convention is always 5′ on the left.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: In the B-DNA double helix, base pairs stack {{c1::0.34 nm::distance}} apart, with {{c1::10::bp per turn}} base pairs per full 360° turn.
Back Extra: Distinguish: DNA inside cells averages 10.4 base pairs per turn — the textbook 10 is the idealized model.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The two sugar-phosphate backbones of a double helix run in opposite directions — one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′ — a relationship called {{c1::antiparallel::orientation term}}.
Back Extra: Why: this opposite chemical polarity shapes how replication, transcription, and recombination must work.

Text: Double-helix stability comes from two forces: the many weak {{c1::hydrogen bonds}} between paired bases, and the hydrophobic {{c1::base-stacking forces}} between adjacent base pairs.
Back Extra: Why: the flat faces of the base pairs are nonpolar, so the stacked core hides from water — in an aqueous cell that insolubility itself holds the helix together.
verified_by: husk_groups cleared post-rewrite: the two c1 spans are cued independently (H-bonds between paired bases vs stacking between adjacent pairs), each cold-solvable with the other hidden

Text: Of the two unequal grooves on the DNA double helix’s surface, the much wider one is the {{c1::major}} groove and the narrower is the {{c1::minor}} groove.
Back Extra: Why: the width difference matters for protein–DNA recognition — some proteins that regulate gene expression bind the major groove; others bind the minor groove.

Text: {{c1::B}}-DNA is the conformation DNA takes under physiological conditions — a {{c2::right::right or left}}-handed helix with about 10 base pairs per turn.
Back Extra: Cue: the vast majority of DNA in living cells is B-form; the Watson–Crick model IS B-DNA.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: {{c1::A}}-DNA forms in high salt or partial dehydration — right-handed like B-DNA but shorter and thicker, with {{c2::11::bp per turn}} base pairs per turn.
Back Extra: Why: pure DNA almost never adopts the A form in vivo — but DNA–RNA heteroduplexes and RNA–RNA duplexes take a very similar structure, which is A-DNA’s real biological relevance.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: {{c1::Z}}-DNA is the {{c2::left::right or left}}-handed double-helical form — named for the {{c1::zigzag}} path of its backbone — occurring in {{c3::G:C-rich}} sequences with alternating purines and pyrimidines, with {{c4::12::bp per turn}} base pairs per turn.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: Z-DNA’s function in living cells is still unclear.

Cue: one single deep groove, and the thinnest helix (1.8 nm) of the three DNA forms.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: Supercoils enter DNA when one or both strands are {{c1::cleaved}}, the ends are {{c1::twisted around each other}}, and — the precondition — the molecule's ends are {{c2::fixed (not free to rotate)}}.
Back Extra: Ex: circular chromosomes fix their own ends; eukaryotic linear DNA is fixed by attachments to non-DNA chromosome components — both can therefore be supercoiled.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: Twisting cut DNA in the same direction as the helix winds produces a {{c1::positive::positive or negative}} supercoil ({{c1::overwound::overwound or underwound}} DNA); twisting opposite to the winding produces a {{c1::negative}} supercoil ({{c1::underwound}} DNA).
Back Extra: Cue: with-the-twist = over; against-the-twist = under.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: In vivo, the functional DNA of almost all organisms is {{c1::negatively::positively or negatively}} supercoiled.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: “almost all” is deliberate — the DNA of certain viruses is the noted exception.

Why: many of a chromosome’s biological functions can be carried out only when its DNA is negatively supercoiled.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: In most viruses and prokaryotes, all the genes reside in {{c1::a single chromosome}} consisting of {{c1::one molecule of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA)}}.
Back Extra: Ex: bacteriophage MS2 packs its whole genome — 4 genes — into one 3569-nucleotide RNA molecule, while the largest DNA viruses (phage T2, the animal pox viruses) carry about 150 genes.

Text: Not every DNA genome is double-stranded: bacteriophage {{c1::ΦX174::phage}} packages its genome as single-stranded DNA.
Back Extra:
Cue: 5386 nucleotides, 11 genes — the ultimate in genetic economy.

Pitfall: single-strandedness is why Chargaff arithmetic fails on ΦX174.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: The E. coli K12 genome is {{c1::4.6 million::number}} base pairs of DNA.
Back Extra: Distinguish: prokaryotic genomes generally run from just under 2 million to over 5 million base pairs, carrying roughly 2000–5000 genes.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The E. coli chromosome's circular DNA has a contour length of about {{c1::1500 μm::length}} — packed into a cell only 1–2 μm across.
Back Extra: Why: a molecule ~1000× longer than its container forces an extremely condensed, folded state.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The functional state of a bacterial chromosome is the {{c1::folded genome}}: the DNA is organized into {{c2::50 to 100::how many}} loops (domains), each one {{c3::independently negatively supercoiled}}.
Back Extra: Cue: RNA and protein are both structural components of the folded genome — it is not naked DNA.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text:
Enzyme probes dissect the bacterial folded genome:

One single-strand DNase nick → relaxes {{c1::only the nicked domain::one domain or all}}

RNase → {{c1::unfolds the loops; supercoiling unchanged}}
Back Extra: Why: supercoiling is per-domain (so a nick relaxes locally), while the folding itself hangs on RNA anchors — cut those and the loops open, still supercoiled.

Text: The compaction of a chromosome's material into a much smaller volume for mitosis or meiosis is called {{c1::condensation}}.
Back Extra:
Why: tight metaphase packaging eases segregation into daughter nuclei and keeps chromosomes from tangling and breaking.

Cue: interphase chromosomes are metabolically active but nearly invisible; metaphase chromosomes are thick, visible bodies on the spindle.

Text: Chemical analysis shows chromatin consists primarily of {{c1::DNA}} and {{c1::proteins}}, with lesser amounts of {{c1::RNA}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: histone content tracks DNA content — a constant, conserved histone:DNA ratio across eukaryotes — while the nonhistone fraction varies widely among cell types.

Cue: chromatin is the DNA–protein complex present in nuclei.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: Chromatin's proteins fall into two classes: the basic, positively charged {{c1::histones}}, and the heterogeneous, largely acidic {{c1::nonhistone chromosomal proteins}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: histones = packaging hardware, nearly identical everywhere; nonhistones = diverse, cell-type-specific — the likely gene regulators.

Text: All plants and animals have five histone types: {{c1::H1, H2a, H2b, H3, and H4::5 names}}.
Back Extra: Cue: four of them (H2a, H2b, H3, H4) build the nucleosome core; H1 works outside it.

Text: The five histones occur in molar ratios of approximately {{c1::1 H1 : 2 H2a : 2 H2b : 2 H3 : 2 H4::ratio}}.
Back Extra: Why: the 2:2:2:2 stoichiometry is the octamer — two of each core histone per nucleosome — with a single H1 per complete nucleosome.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run; bloated_blank cleared: the ratio is one numeric chunk recalled as a unit, hint labels it

Text: Histones are basic because {{c3::20 to 30::percent}}% of their amino acids are {{c1::arginine and lysine::2 amino acids}} — their positive charges grip DNA's negatively charged {{c2::phosphate}} backbone.
Back Extra: Mechanism: exposed –NH₃⁺ groups make histones polycations; DNA is a polyanion — electrostatic attraction does the binding.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Histone exception: in some {{c1::sperm::cell type}}, histones are replaced by another class of small basic proteins called {{c2::protamines}}.
Back Extra: Cue: almost every other cell type in plants and animals keeps the standard five histones.

Text: The nearly invariant core histones fit a {{c1::structural / DNA-packaging::structural or regulatory}} role; the widely varying nonhistone proteins fit a {{c1::gene-regulatory::structural or regulatory}} role.
Back Extra: Why: a protein doing the same mechanical job everywhere cannot afford to change; regulators must differ between cell types precisely because gene expression differs.

Text: Each eukaryotic chromosome consists of {{c1::one single, giant DNA molecule::how many DNA molecules}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: gaps in a chromosome's assembled sequence do not prove separate molecules — long repetitive arrays simply defeat current sequencing technology.

Text: Kavenoff and Zimm sized the largest Drosophila DNA by its stretch-relaxation behavior in solution; the result was unchanged by treatment with {{c1::pronase (a protein-degrading enzyme)::treatment}} — ruling out {{c2::separate DNA segments joined by protein linkers}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the time a stretched DNA coil takes to relax scales with molecule size; the largest molecule matched the whole chromosome's DNA content — with or without its proteins.

Ex: a strain whose largest chromosome carried a relocated centromere gave the same result — the DNA molecule is continuous through the centromere.

Text: Gently isolated interphase chromatin looks like beads on a string: ellipsoidal beads about {{c1::11 nm::diameter}} across — the {{c2::nucleosomes}} — joined by thin threads of nuclease-sensitive {{c2::linker DNA}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the beads protect their DNA from nucleases; the exposed linkers between them are where nucleases cut.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Partial nuclease digestion of chromatin releases DNA fragments in discrete sizes that are {{c1::integral multiples of the smallest fragment::size pattern}} — evidence that chromatin has a repeating structural unit.
Back Extra: Why: protected DNA comes in fixed-size packets (nucleosomes); cutting different numbers of exposed linkers yields 1×, 2×, 3×… packet sizes.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: The nucleosome core is {{c1::146::bp count}} nucleotide pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer — two molecules each of {{c2::H2a, H2b, H3, and H4::4 histones}}.
Back Extra: Cue: extensive nuclease digestion chews everything except this protected 146-bp core particle.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: In the nucleosome core, the DNA winds {{c1::1.65::number of turns}} times around the outside of the histone octamer as a negative superhelix.
Back Extra: Cue: X-ray diffraction at 0.28-nm resolution located all eight histones and the wound DNA precisely.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The complete nucleosome contains {{c1::166::bp count}} nucleotide pairs — two full superhelical turns — stabilized by one molecule of {{c2::histone H1::which histone}} bound to the outside of the structure.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the core alone is 146 bp and involves only the octamer histones — H1 is NOT part of the octamer.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The linker DNA between nucleosome cores varies in length from species to species and cell type to cell type — reported linkers run from {{c1::8 to 114::range, bp}} nucleotide pairs.
Back Extra: Cue: the cores are invariant; the linkers are where the variability lives.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The chromatin fibers of metaphase chromosomes average {{c1::30 nm::diameter}} in diameter — formed by condensing the 11-nm nucleosome fiber.
Back Extra: Cue: carefully isolated interphase chromatin shows the same 30-nm fibers — the light microscope simply sees where they pack tightly.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: The two competing models for the 30-nm fiber's substructure are the {{c1::solenoid}} model and the {{c1::zigzag}} model.
Back Extra: Cue: the zigzag appears when chromatin is cryopreserved (quick-frozen) rather than chemically fixed; which structure exists in vivo — or whether both do — is still uncertain.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text:
Eukaryotic DNA is packaged through three levels of condensation:

Level 1 — DNA wound into nucleosomes → {{c1::the 11-nm interphase chromatin fiber}}

Level 2 — folding/supercoiling with histone H1 → {{c1::the 30-nm chromatin fiber}}

Level 3 — nonhistone scaffold → {{c1::supercoiled loops/domains of the metaphase chromosome}}
Back Extra:
Cue: naked DNA → 11-nm beads → 30-nm fiber → scaffold-anchored loops — packing 10³–10⁵ μm of DNA into a metaphase structure a few μm long.

Roster: Level 1 = 11-nm nucleosome fiber · Level 2 = 30-nm fiber (H1) · Level 3 = scaffold loops → metaphase chromosome.
verified_by: agent, claims verified against full page text when selecting coverage marks this run

Text: The central core of a metaphase chromosome — the {{c1::scaffold}} — is composed of {{c2::nonhistone::histone or nonhistone}} chromosomal proteins.
Back Extra: Ex: strip the histones from an isolated metaphase chromosome and the scaffold remains, surrounded by a huge halo of DNA.

Text: The human genome has about {{c1::700::factor}}× more DNA than E. coli's but only {{c1::4.5::factor}}× more genes — because {{c2::human genes are larger}} and {{c2::much human DNA is nongenic (not in genes)}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the nongenic majority was once dismissed as “junk” DNA — now known to matter for chromosome structure.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: In density-gradient centrifugation, the genomic fractions that settle away from the main band (because they are G:C- or A:T-rich) are called {{c1::satellite DNAs}} — {{c2::short sequences repeated over and over::composition}}.
Back Extra: Cue: from Latin satelles, “attendant” — side bands attending the main band.

Text: In density-gradient centrifugation, G:C-rich DNA comes to rest {{c1::lower::higher or lower}} than typical DNA, and A:T-rich DNA {{c1::higher::higher or lower}}.
Back Extra: Why: G:C pairs hold three hydrogen bonds to A:T's two — the tighter bonding makes G:C-rich DNA denser.

Text: Heating DNA to near {{c2::100}}°C separates its strands — {{c1::denaturation}}; cooling slowly lets complementary strands re-form double helices — {{c1::renaturation}}.
Back Extra: Why: heat breaks the many weak hydrogen bonds; slow cooling gives complements time to find each other.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: In a renaturation experiment, repetitive DNA sequences re-form duplexes {{c1::faster::faster or slower}} than unique sequences do.
Back Extra:
Why: renaturation rate tracks concentration, and repeats are present many times over — relatively more concentrated than unique sequences.

Cue: the rate difference lets researchers isolate repetitive DNA and estimate its degree of repetition.

Text: The number of times a sequence is repeated in a genome is its {{c1::copy number}}; highly repetitive (satellite) sequences reach {{c2::10³ to 10⁶::range}} copies.
Back Extra: Distinguish: eukaryotic genomes are a mix of unique, moderately repetitive, and highly repetitive sequence classes — unique sequences hold most of the genes.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Exception to “genes are unique sequences”: the {{c1::ribosomal RNA::which RNA}} genes are highly redundant — hundreds or even thousands of copies per genome.
Back Extra: Why: cells carry enormous numbers of ribosomes, so rRNA demand outstrips what single-copy genes could supply.

Text: {{c1::In situ hybridization}} finds a sequence's chromosomal home: a labeled single-stranded {{c2::probe}} renatures with its complement in chromosomes spread on a slide, and the label (usually a fluorescent dye) marks the spot.
Back Extra: Cue: Latin “in position” — the hybrid forms exactly where the complement naturally sits; this is the basis of chromosome painting.

Text: Highly repetitive DNA is concentrated primarily in the regions around the {{c1::centromeres::chromosome landmark}} of eukaryotic chromosomes.
Back Extra: Distinguish: less highly repetitive sequences sit out in the chromosome arms — some in tandem arrays, others dispersed (many of those dispersed ones are mobile transposons).

Text: Transposable elements (transposons) and their derivatives make up about {{c1::44::percent}}% of the human genome.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: ~15% in Drosophila melanogaster; over 80% in maize.

Cue: dispersed repetitive sequences that can move to new genomic positions.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Spindle microtubules attach to a chromosome at its {{c1::kinetochores}} — complex protein structures assembled on the {{c2::centromeres}} of the sister chromatids.
Back Extra: Why: that attachment is what moves sister chromatids to opposite poles — the basis of proper disjunction in mitosis and meiosis.

Text: A chromosome or fragment that lacks a centromere is usually {{c1::lost::its fate}} during cell division.
Back Extra: Why: with nothing for spindle microtubules to grab, the fragment cannot be pulled into either daughter nucleus.

Text: The simplest known centromeres belong to {{c1::yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)::organism}} — a DNA segment only {{c2::125::bp count}} base pairs long is sufficient for proper mitotic behavior.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the centromeres of multicellular plants and animals span thousands to millions of base pairs of repetitive DNA.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Human centromeres are built of long tandem arrays of the {{c1::alpha satellite}} sequence — a {{c2::171::bp count}}-bp repeat present in {{c3::5000 to 15,000::copy range}} copies per centromere.
Back Extra: Cue: whole centromeres run 500,000 to 1.5 million bp — these massive repeat arrays are exactly why centromeric DNA resisted sequencing.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: {{c1::Heterochromatin}} stains deeply and is packaged more tightly; {{c1::euchromatin}} stains less deeply and is looser.
Back Extra: Ex: centromeres and their flanking (pericentric) regions are heterochromatin — mostly repetitive, though some genes (e.g., rRNA gene arrays in Drosophila) live there.

Text: The centromere-marking protein {{c1::CENP-A::protein}} is a variant of histone {{c2::H3::which histone}} that binds eukaryotic centromeres — even yeast's tiny ones.
Back Extra: Cue: in complex centromeres a methylated H3 is present too, and Heterochromatin Protein 1 (HP1) may help package the region.

Text: The specialized structures at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes are the {{c1::telomeres}} — the term was coined in {{c2::1938::year}} by {{c2::Hermann J. Muller::person}}.
Back Extra:
Parts: telo- (Greek telos, end) + -mere (meros, part) — literally “end part.”

Cue: prokaryotes' circular chromosomes have no ends, so they need no telomeres.

Text:
Telomeres serve three functions:

{{c1::block nuclease degradation of the chromosome ends}}

{{c1::prevent the ends from fusing with other DNA}}

{{c1::let the ends replicate without loss of material}}
Back Extra: Cue: protect · don't stick · finish copying.

Text: The telomere repeat unit of humans — and vertebrates generally — is {{c1::TTAGGG::6 bases}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Tetrahymena uses TTGGGG; Arabidopsis uses TTTAGGG — the general pattern is 5′ T(1–4) A(0–1) G(1–8) 3′.

Cue: conserved across 100+ vertebrate species, from fishes to mammals.

Text: Normal human somatic telomeres contain {{c3::500 to 3000::repeat count}} TTAGGG repeats and gradually {{c1::shorten::shorten or lengthen}} with age — but the telomeres of {{c2::germ-line cells and cancer cells::2 cell types}} do not.
Back Extra:
Why: gradual shortening ties telomere length to human aging.

Cue: repeat number varies by species, by chromosome, and even by cell type on the same chromosome.
verified_by: agent, read from page text this run

Text: Most telomeres end in a G-rich, single-stranded {{c1::3′::3′ or 5′}} overhang, which can invade an upstream stretch of telomere repeats and pair with the complementary strand — forming a protective loop called a {{c2::t-loop}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: human 3′ overhangs run 50–500 bases (ciliates': only 12–16).

Why: tucking the free end away hides it from nucleases and repair enzymes.

Text: Telomeric DNA is coated and protected by the {{c3::six::number of proteins}}-protein complex {{c1::shelterin}}: {{c2::TRF1 and TRF2}} bind the double-stranded repeats, while {{c2::POT1}} binds the single-stranded overhang.
Back Extra:
Cue: TIN2 and TPP1 tether POT1 to the TRFs, and TRF2-associated Rap1 helps regulate telomere length.

Why: shelterin shields telomeric DNA from degradation and from being “repaired” as damage.

Text: A chromosome is {{c1::one packaged unit of a cell's DNA}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “Chromosomes are composed of two types of large organic molecules (macromolecules): nucleic acids and proteins.”

Distinguish: chromatin is the DNA–protein material in its loose working form; a chromosome is the organized, countable package.

Formal: “darkly staining nucleoprotein bodies observed in cells during division; each carries a linear array of genes.”

Text: A nucleic acid is {{c1::an information-carrying macromolecule built of nucleotide chains}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “Chromosomes are composed of two types of large organic molecules: nucleic acids and proteins.”

Cue: the two kinds are DNA and RNA.

Formal: “a macromolecule composed of phosphoric acid, pentose sugar, and organic bases.”

Text: A protein is {{c1::a macromolecule made of amino-acid (polypeptide) chains}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “Chromosomes are composed of two types of large organic molecules: nucleic acids and proteins.”

Distinguish: in chromosomes, proteins do the packaging — the nucleic acids carry the genetic information.

Text: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is {{c1::the usually double-stranded nucleic acid storing genetic information}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “There are two types of nucleic acids: deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA).”

Distinguish: RNA is usually single-stranded, uses the sugar ribose, and swaps thymine for uracil.

Text: RNA (ribonucleic acid) is {{c1::a usually single-stranded nucleic acid}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “There are two types of nucleic acids: deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA).”

Distinguish: DNA is double-stranded, uses deoxyribose, and keeps thymine where RNA uses uracil.

Cue: in some viruses, RNA — not DNA — is the genetic material.

Text: In the pneumococcus transformation experiments, Type IIIS is {{c1::the virulent, capsule-bearing strain}}.
Back Extra:

Text: In the pneumococcus transformation experiments, Type IIR is {{c1::the avirulent strain lacking a capsule}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: “…and living Type IIR bacteria (avirulent) into mice…”

Distinguish: Type IIIS = capsule, virulent. IIR is the safe strain that the transforming principle converts into a killer.

Text: In vitro means {{c1::“within glass” — outside a living organism}}.

Ex: “In 1931, Richard Sia and Martin Dawson analyzed this genetic transformation in vitro, and showed that the mice played no role.”

Text: Deoxyribonuclease (DNase) is {{c1::an enzyme that cuts up DNA}}.

Text: Ribonuclease (RNase) is {{c1::an enzyme that cuts up RNA}}.

Text: Bacteriophage T2 is {{c1::a virus that infects E. coli bacteria}}.

Text: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is {{c1::a plant virus: RNA in a protein coat}}.

Text: Genotypically means {{c1::in terms of genetic makeup}}.

Text: Chromatin is {{c1::the DNA–protein complex that chromosomes are made of}}.
